extracted.intended_audience: researchers, peer-review practitioners (NIH reviewers/SROs), and policymakers interested in grant peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards describing how NIH-style study sections evaluate grant applications: the scoring scales, the five review criteria, reviewer roles and meeting workflow, triage rules, and discourse (Score Calibration Talk) that shapes scoring. Useful for analyzing or designing peer review panels for research grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse nine-point scoring rubric (NIH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers employ a reverse nine-point scale, with each number corresponding to a single descriptive adjective (figure adapted from NIH 2015). Preliminary and final reviewer scores range from 1 to 9; Final Panel Scores are the average of all panelists' scores multiplied by 10 (range 10–90).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mapping of numbers to adjectives is intentionally ambiguous so reviewers can apply expert judgment; ambiguity can increase subjective variability. See Fig.1 for the adapted rubric. Numeric scales: preliminary/final reviewer scores = 1–9; final panel scores = 10–90 (average*10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers evaluate each application on five criteria: significance, investigator qualifications, innovation, methodological approach, and research environment (plus a holistic overall impact impression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers provide preliminary scores for each of the five criteria and an overall score. Critiques should address strengths and weaknesses relative to these criteria, and the overall impact statement synthesizes how these aspects affect the application's likely scientific impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough written critique and overall impact statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to meetings, reviewers are responsible for reading assigned applications and writing a thorough critique of strengths and weaknesses, including a holistic impression of overall impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written critiques should justify numeric scores by detailing strengths/weaknesses and connecting them to overall impact and the five criteria; these critiques guide the panel discussion and provide public accounting for scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary scoring and SRO averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Three assigned reviewers provide preliminary scores for the five criteria and an overall score; the Scientific Review Officer (SRO) calculates the average preliminary score across the three assigned reviewers for each application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SRO uses the average preliminary score to determine the order of review (strongest first). This preliminary average determines which applications enter discussion (top 50%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage rule (top 50% discussed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the top 50% of applications, based on average preliminary score, are discussed during the meeting; the bottom half are 'triaged' and not discussed further (and thus not considered for funding in that meeting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triage is a formal gate: only discussed applications receive final scores. Analyses of scoring behavior typically focus on discussed applications because final reviewer and panel scores exist only for those.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer assignment roles (primary/secondary/tertiary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each application in a panel has three assigned reviewers designated primary, secondary, and tertiary based on the relevance of each reviewer's expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary reviewer has the most relevant expertise and typically leads the summary; the SRO assigns designations and balances expertise across panels. Reviewer assignment affects whose critique and score anchor the discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final scoring and panel averaging procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: After discussion, the three assigned reviewers publicly announce their final scores; non-assigned panelists privately record their final scores. The Final Panel Score is the average of all panelists' scores multiplied by 10 (10–90).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are as many final scores as there are panel members. Final Panel Scores, not preliminary reviewer averages, are used by governance to inform funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score range and deviation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest and highest of the three assigned reviewers' final scores constitute the 'score range' for that application; non-assigned panelists' scores are expected to fall within this range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a panelist's score falls outside the announced range, they are expected to announce that fact and may provide rationale for the divergence. This protocol structures accountability and potential justifications for outlying judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to disclose any institutional or other conflicts of interest with an application, following standard NIH practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is required prior to participating; conflicts affect assignment and participation and are part of SRO oversight to preserve fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-identification and use of provided materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications were de-identified (names replaced with pseudonyms; identifying information removed) and reviewers were instructed to refer only to the materials sent to them to reduce effects of prior knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting reviewers to provided materials and de-identifying content is intended to reduce bias from prior familiarity and maintain confidentiality; this is standard practice in controlled/constructed study sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting workflow and roles (SRO, chair, score-reporting sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meetings begin with the SRO's opening remarks and review of the scoring system; the chair introduces each application, the three assigned reviewers state preliminary scores (score-reporting sequence) and summarize critiques, followed by panel discussion; chair summarizes and calls for final scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structured sequence (opening, score-reporting, summary, discussion, summary, final scores) provides procedural consistency. Chairs and the SRO mediate discussion, summarize critiques, and enforce scoring norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocation per application
rubrics_metrics.description: Meetings were timed to ensure panels spent approximately 15 minutes reviewing each application, simulating the time pressure of actual NIH study sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time pressure is a key contextual factor influencing how deeply panels discuss applications and how much SCT (score calibration talk) can occur; realistic timing is important for ecological validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and reviewer load norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical standing NIH study sections roster 18–21 reviewers; ad hoc panels or Special Emphasis Panels may have 8–10 reviewers. Reviewer assignment loads vary (standing study sections: ~9–10 apps; ad hoc panels: as few as 5–6); CSS panels in study targeted ~12 reviewers (videoconference panel had 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel size and reviewer load influence breadth of discussion, number of final scores, and time per application—important design parameters when evaluating reliability and generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score Calibration Talk (SCT) as a discourse metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Score Calibration Talk is any discourse during panel meetings related to scores or scoring norms that helps establish common ground around numeric meanings; SCT was analyzed as a factor influencing scoring variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SCT instances were exhaustively coded and timed; presence, frequency, and type of SCT (self- or other-initiated) correlate with within-panel convergence and between-panel divergence in scores. SCT is both a descriptive phenomenon and a potential target for interventions to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-initiated SCT (S-SCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: S-SCT: any instance where a reviewer mentions their score (word or number) along with an account (rationale/justification) for that score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely stating a score without a rationale is not S-SCT. S-SCT provides public access to a reviewer's interpretation of numeric scores and offers a space for others to agree or disagree—thereby promoting common ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other-initiated SCT (O-SCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: O-SCT: any instance where a panelist calls on other reviewers to account for their scoring practices, typically by challenging a score (e.g., known-answer or challenging questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: O-SCT can be brief or extended; it functions as a mechanism to prompt justification and can shape the direction and length of discussion. Examples include explicit challenges like 'Your comments are meaner than your score.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability metric and thresholds (Krippendorff's α)
rubrics_metrics.description: Krippendorff's α was used to quantify agreement; values above 0.80 are considered 'reliable' and 0.67–0.80 suitable for tentative conclusions (Krippendorff 2004).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Krippendorff's α accommodates multiple raters and missing values and was applied to preliminary reviewer scores, final reviewer scores, and final panel scores for intra-panel and inter-panel agreement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting format as a variable (face-to-face vs videoconference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting format (in-person face-to-face vs video-assisted/videoconference) can affect dynamics; the study included three in-person panels and one videoconference panel to explore differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Video-assisted meetings may be smaller and may produce different amounts/kinds of SCT and different agreement patterns; format is a design consideration when evaluating peer review reliability and generalizability.
